title: Deep throat & back-of-tongue: ع غ ف ق
objectives: Student can identify and pronounce ع, غ, ف, ق in isolation on sight.
Student can produce ع without collapsing it into ء (hamza/glottal stop).
Student can distinguish ق from ك (introduced next lesson, previewed today as the contrast target).

slides.heading: Lesson 1.5 — Deep throat & back-of-tongue: ع غ ف ق
Cumulative recap — all 17 letters so far

audio.cue: ا: an open, unobstructed sound from deep in the chest cavity — no closure anywhere, just a clear open vowel
lips fully together
tongue-tip on gum ridge
tongue between teeth
ح: a strong, breathy, unvoiced friction from the middle of the throat — like fogging a mirror from deep in the throat, no English equivalent
خ: a rasping fricative from the upper throat/back of the tongue against the soft palate — a genuine back-of-throat 'kh', not softened
د: tongue-tip taps the upper gum ridge firmly — a plain, crisp 'd'
ذ: tongue-tip between the teeth, same point as ث but VOICED — 'th' as in 'this', never a 'z'

audio.title: Arabic101 Makharij Lesson 10 — ر (ra), the ULTIMATE guide

audio.cue: ز: tip of tongue near the lower teeth, a plain buzzing 'z' — voiced twin of س
س: tip of tongue near the lower teeth, a thin hiss — a plain 's'
ش: middle of tongue against the roof of the mouth, a soft 'sh'
ع: a mid-throat muscular squeeze, voiced — no equivalent sound in English or Turkic languages

notes: A mid-throat muscular squeeze/constriction, voiced — genuinely has no equivalent in English or Turkic languages
Contrast against a plain glottal stop (ء) — the difference is a real muscular squeeze, not just "starting a vowel abruptly"

slides.heading: Guided ع drill — throat-squeeze vs glottal stop
slides.instructions: Repeat after your teacher: the throat-squeeze of ع, contrasted against a plain glottal stop (ء — just a quick aside here, not yet formally taught). Listen for the difference — a real muscular squeeze, not just "starting a vowel abruptly".

audio.cue: ع: a mid-throat muscular squeeze, voiced — no equivalent sound in English or Turkic languages
a plain glottal stop — like the catch in "uh-oh" — no throat-muscle squeeze, just a stop of the breath
غ: upper throat, same zone as خ but voiced — a uvular fricative, like a French uvular 'r'

slides.makhraj: upper throat, same zone as خ but voiced
notes: A uvular fricative, described as close to a French uvular "r" — must stay a fricative, not a stop
Same origin point as خ (lesson 1.2) — only voicing differs

slides.heading: غ vs خ — minimal-pair listening
slides.instructions: Your teacher says either غ or خ — find which one you heard and point to it. This tests the voiced/unvoiced distinction at the same throat zone.

audio.cue: غ: upper throat, same zone as خ but voiced — a uvular fricative, like a French uvular 'r'
خ: a rasping fricative from the upper throat/back of the tongue against the soft palate — a genuine back-of-throat 'kh', not softened
ف: inner lower lip against the edge of the upper front teeth — a plain 'f'

slides.makhraj: inner lower lip against the edge of the upper front teeth
notes: Usually low-risk, but don't let "easy-looking" letters get sloppy articulation just because they're comfortable

slides.makhraj: back of tongue against the soft palate
notes: A deep, uvular "cough-like" stop from the very back of the tongue — heavier and further back than ك (next lesson)
قال (he said) vs a ك-flattened version is a genuine meaning-changing mix-up

slides.heading: Preview-contrast: ق vs ك
slides.instructions: ك is not formally taught until next lesson, but don't flatten ق into it — listen to both letters, then pronounce ق keeping it deep and uvular. قال (he said) vs a ك-flattened version is a genuine meaning-changing mix-up, so precision matters here.

audio.cue: ك: back of tongue against the soft palate, shallower in the mouth than ق — a plain 'k'

script: Open with a cumulative cold-call of all 17 letters learned so far before introducing ع.
Model ع as a genuine mid-throat muscular squeeze, explicitly contrasted against a plain glottal stop — this has no equivalent in English or Turkic languages.
Give ع the highest-priority correction time in the lesson; per the sourced research it is commonly flattened toward ء.
Use the قال/كال (he said / he measured) meaning-changing pair as a concrete teaching moment when previewing ق vs ك.
Don't let ف get sloppy just because it's comfortable — easy-looking letters deserve real articulation too.
listenFor: ع substituted with ء — flattening the muscular throat-squeeze into a plain glottal stop, described in the sourced research as happening because "no equivalent phoneme exists in English or Turkic languages" (teaching-mistakes-assessment.md A.1). This is the single highest-priority correction in this lesson.
غ confused with خ, or blended toward ق — same-zone voicing confusion (A.1).
ق flattened to plain ك — loses its deep uvular quality (A.4); use the قال/كال (he said / he measured) meaning-changing pair as a concrete teaching moment for why precision matters here.
ف — usually low-risk, but do not let "easy-looking" letters get sloppy articulation just because they're comfortable (per Arabic101's own framing of lesson 14's "easy letters with tricky mistakes").
